_comment: Which IFC classes each Project Delivery element name covers, for element
names that appear only in the per-typology delivery sheets. Names the
delivery sheets share with the IFC+SG standard (Wall, Door, Column...)
are not repeated here -- they resolve through ifc_sg_classes.json.
Like ifc_sg_classes.json, this is NOT extracted from the workbook: the
standard's own mechanism for recording the class is the modeller-declared
IfcExportAs parameter, so every entry is a judgement call kept as data.
Entries with an empty 'classes' list are deliberately unmapped, with the
reason given -- silently attaching the wrong parameter set is worse than
One constraint has no counterpart in the base file: within any single
typology, a plain class name may belong to at most one element name, or
an element created as that class could not be told which parameter set
it owes. Qualified 'Class/PREDEFINEDTYPE' entries (see the base file's
comment) share a class where the type can tell claimants apart; several
entries here are unmapped because it cannot. requirements.py enforces
the constraint at load time and refuses both claimants rather than

Accessories & Routing (Service Routing).review: Industrial carries this alongside plain 'Accessories & Routing', and the split is procurement scope, not anything an IFC class expresses. Mapping both to the routing classes would double-attach.

Casework / Joinery.review: Built-in joinery usually exports as IfcFurniture, but Industrial (the one typology using this name) claims IfcFurniture for 'Furniture' already.

Equipment (Primary).review: The primary/secondary split is a procurement distinction with no IFC counterpart; mapping both to the equipment classes would attach two parameter sets to every pump.

Finish.review: Floor and wall finishes, by PredefinedType; Industrial's plain IfcCovering stays with 'Ceiling'. Coverings typed neither way get the ceiling set, which may be wrong for an untyped finish.

Finishes.review: Healthcare (the one typology using this name) has no separate Ceiling element, so coverings there carry the finishes requirements. Wrong if a project models ceilings as coverings without meaning 'finish'.

Fixture / Device.review: Read as the electrical fixtures-and-devices categories. The typologies using this name (Retail, Private Residential) carry no 'Terminal' or 'Equipment' element, so these classes are unclaimed there -- but the reading itself is a judgement.

Generic Model.note: The name is authoring-tool vocabulary; a proxy is exactly what a generic model exports as.

Infrastructure.review: Road and rail assets are IFC4.3 alignment-domain classes (IfcRoad, IfcRailway, IfcCourse...), out of reach of an IFC4 project. Revisit when Bonsai projects here move to 4.3.

Railing / Balustrade.note: Industrial's singular spelling of the base 'Railings / Balustrade'.

Services Routing.review: Retail and Private Residential's name for what the base data calls 'Accessories & Routing'; same classes, same breadth caveat.

Setting Up & Project Information.note: Project-level metadata, not a physical element -- same as the base 'Setting up & Project Information'.

Site (External Works).review: Same ground as the base 'External Works', which is deliberately unmapped: it spans drains, kerbs, road furniture and boundaries with no one class.

Space Allocation.note: Industrial's name for the base 'Spatial Allocation'. Spatial, not physical: classified through Bonsai's spatial workflow, not the drawing tools.

Specialty Equipment.review: Usually exported as proxies, but Industrial claims IfcBuildingElementProxy for 'Generic Model' already.

Terminal (Fixture and Device).review: Industrial carries plain 'Terminal' too; the parenthetical scope is not expressible by class.
